items.pronunciation_notes: The ऐ is a single open vowel, so है sounds like English 'hey' said flat — not like 'high'.

learn.explanation_en: Sentences that link two things — this is a book, the tea is hot — end in a form of होना. है is the form for a single third person: he, she, it, or any one noun. The thing to notice first is not the verb but its position: it comes at the very end of the sentence, after everything else. English speakers reach for the verb far too early and produce word orders that no one uses.

examples.note: The verb comes last, after both nouns.
The adjective comes before the verb, not after it.
बड़ा takes -ा because घर is masculine.

common_error.why_en: The verb goes at the end of a Hindi sentence, never at the front.

practice.question: चाय गरम ___।
practice.explanation_en: चाय is a single third person, so the verb is है.

game.explanation_en: One book is a single third person, so only है fits. हूँ belongs to मैं and हो to तुम.

items.pronunciation_notes: The dot nasalises the vowel, so हैं differs from है by a hum rather than by any extra consonant.
items.gloss_en: are — third person plural, and respectful singular

learn.explanation_en: हैं is the plural of है, used when the subject is more than one. It also does a second job: a single person spoken of respectfully takes हैं rather than है, which is why आप — the polite 'you' — always takes हैं even when you are addressing one person. In writing the only difference is the dot; in speech it is a nasalised vowel and easy to miss.

examples.note: A plural subject takes a plural verb.
छोटा takes -े for a masculine plural.
आप takes हैं even when only one person is meant.

common_error.why_en: The subject is plural, so the verb needs the dot.

practice.question: ये किताबें ___।
practice.explanation_en: किताबें is plural, so the verb is हैं.

game.explanation_en: बच्चे is plural, so the verb must be हैं rather than है.

items.pronunciation_notes: The crescent nasalises the long vowel, so the word ends in a hum with no n sounded: huuṁ.

learn.explanation_en: हूँ goes with मैं, meaning I, and with nothing else at all. Hindi verbs change shape according to who the subject is, and this is the first of those changes. Because the form belongs to मैं alone, the pronoun is very often dropped — यहाँ हूँ already means 'I am here' without anything further. Leaving it out is normal rather than casual.

examples.note: यहाँ never changes form.
खुश does not change, whoever is speaking.
A male speaker says बड़ा; a female speaker says बड़ी.

common_error.why_en: मैं takes हूँ. है belongs to the third person only.

practice.question: मैं यहाँ ___।
practice.explanation_en: मैं takes हूँ, and no other subject does.

game.explanation_en: मैं pairs only with हूँ. The other three belong to other subjects.

summary.recap_en: This level built the first Hindi sentences. They end in a form of होना, and which form you use depends on the subject: one third person takes है, a plural or respected one takes हैं, and मैं takes हूँ.
summary.next_up_en: Next: हो completes the present forms, and the four are set out as a set.

items.pronunciation_notes: A flat ओ with no glide at the end: ho, one syllable.

learn.explanation_en: हो is the form that goes with तुम, the everyday 'you' used with friends, family and people of about your own age. It is short and easy to lose in fast speech, so listen for it. Note that it looks identical to हो inside होना — position is the only thing that tells you which one you are reading.

examples.note: The question word comes before the verb.
तुम takes plural agreement even for one person.
खुश does not change form.

common_error.why_en: तुम takes हो. हैं belongs with आप and with plural third persons.

practice.question: तुम कहाँ ___?
practice.explanation_en: तुम takes हो, and nothing else does.

game.explanation_en: तुम pairs only with हो. हैं would be right for आप, but not here.

items.pronunciation_notes: Two of the four carry a nasal — हूँ with a crescent and हैं with a dot — and in both the nasal is a hum rather than a consonant.
items.gloss_en: the four present forms of होना

learn.explanation_en: होना has exactly four forms in the present, and which one you use is decided entirely by the subject: मैं takes हूँ, तुम takes हो, one third person takes है, and everything plural — along with आप — takes हैं. There is no fifth form and no exceptions. Notice what is absent from that list: gender. The present tense of होना does not care whether the subject is masculine or feminine, which is about to change when you meet the past.

examples.note: Two forms, each belonging to one subject only.
Singular and plural in the third person.
आप always takes हैं, however many people are meant.

common_error.why_en: Each subject has exactly one form, and मैं never takes हैं.

practice.question: आप कैसे ___?
practice.explanation_en: आप takes हैं, whether you are addressing one person or several.

game.question_en: Which pairing of subject and verb is correct?
game.explanation_en: वह takes है. मैं needs हूँ, तुम needs हो, and आप needs हैं.

items.pronunciation_notes: The dot is the whole difference, and in speech it nasalises the vowel rather than adding a sound of its own.

learn.explanation_en: The choice between है and हैं is decided by the subject and by nothing else in the sentence. One chair takes है; several chairs take हैं. English does the same thing, so the rule itself is familiar — but Hindi puts the verb at the very end, which means you make the decision several words after the subject has gone past. That gap is where the mistakes happen.

examples.note: One thing, so है.
More than one, so हैं.
साफ़ hides the number, but मेज़ is singular and settles it.

common_error.why_en: The subject is plural, so the verb must be plural too.

practice.question: यह कुर्सी ___।
practice.explanation_en: One chair is singular, so the verb is है.

game.explanation_en: Everything has to agree: ये for a plural, कुर्सियाँ for the plural noun, and हैं for the verb.

summary.recap_en: This level completed the present forms of होना. Four forms, decided by the subject alone: हूँ with मैं, हो with तुम, है with one third person, हैं with anything plural or respected. Gender plays no part.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the past tense, where gender starts to matter.

items.pronunciation_notes: An aspirated dental थ — tongue against the teeth with breath released, and not the th of English 'think'.

learn.explanation_en: था is the past of है for a single masculine subject. Here Hindi does something the present tense never did: the past forms of होना change for gender as well as number. था goes with a masculine singular subject and थी with a feminine one. This is the first time gender has reached into a verb, and from this point onwards it keeps doing so — which is why the last module spent 150 words on it.

examples.note: घर is masculine, so both the adjective and the verb take -ा.
गरम never changes, but था does.
A male speaker says था; a female speaker says थी.

common_error.why_en: चाय is feminine, so the past form has to be थी.

practice.question: घर बड़ा ___।
practice.explanation_en: घर is masculine and singular, so the verb is था.

game.explanation_en: खाना is masculine and singular, so only था fits.

items.pronunciation_notes: The same aspirated dental as था, followed by a long ii: thii.

learn.explanation_en: थी is the feminine counterpart of था, and this is where the gender of every noun you learned starts to have consequences. चाय is feminine, so चाय गरम थी; दूध is masculine, so दूध गरम था. The adjective and the verb both follow the noun, which means one wrong gender costs you two mistakes in a single short sentence rather than one.

examples.note: चाय is feminine, so थी.
Both अच्छी and थी agree with किताब.
रात is feminine despite its consonant ending.

common_error.why_en: किताब is feminine, so both the adjective and the verb take feminine forms.

practice.question: चाय गरम ___।
practice.explanation_en: चाय is feminine and singular, so the verb is थी.

game.explanation_en: किताब is feminine and singular. The adjective is already right in all four, so the verb decides it.

items.pronunciation_notes: A flat ए with no glide, so थे is one clean syllable: the.

learn.explanation_en: थे is the masculine plural past, and like हैं it doubles as the respectful form for one person, so आप always takes थे. It is also the form for a mixed group: if even one member is masculine, the whole group counts as masculine. That rule runs right through the language, and it means थे turns up far more often than its feminine counterpart does.

examples.note: Masculine plural, so both words take -े.
नया becomes नए in the masculine plural.
आप takes थे even when one person is meant.

common_error.why_en: The subject is plural, so both the adjective and the verb take plural forms.

practice.question: बच्चे छोटे ___।
practice.explanation_en: बच्चे is masculine and plural, so the verb is थे.

game.explanation_en: जूते is masculine and plural, so only थे fits.

summary.recap_en: This level introduced the past of होना and the fact that separates it from the present: gender. था goes with a masculine singular, थी with a feminine one, and थे with a masculine plural or with आप.
summary.next_up_en: Next: थीं completes the set, and the two tenses are set side by side.

levels.title_en: थीं, and the two tenses compared

items.pronunciation_notes: The dot nasalises the long vowel, so थीं differs from थी by a hum and nothing more.

learn.explanation_en: थीं is the feminine plural past, and it is the rarest of the four, because a group has to be entirely feminine to take it — one masculine member and the whole thing reverts to थे. In speech the only difference from थी is a nasal hum, so it is easy to miss when listening and easy to leave out when speaking. Notice too that the adjective does not change between the feminine singular and plural, so the verb is often the only thing carrying the number.

examples.note: अच्छी stays the same, but थीं marks the plural.
Noun, adjective and verb are all feminine plural.
खाली never changes, so the verb carries everything.

common_error.why_en: The subject is plural, so the verb needs the dot even though the adjective does not change.

practice.question: किताबें अच्छी ___।
practice.explanation_en: किताबें is feminine and plural, so the verb is थीं.

game.explanation_en: रातें is feminine and plural, so the verb needs both the feminine vowel and the dot.

items.pronunciation_notes: All four open with the same aspirated dental थ; only the vowel and the nasal mark differ.
items.gloss_en: the four past forms of होना

learn.title_en: Four past forms, and why there are four
learn.explanation_en: The present of होना has four forms decided by person: हूँ, हो, है, हैं. The past has four decided by gender and number instead: था, थी, थे, थीं. That is the real difference between the two tenses and it is worth stating plainly — in the past, who is speaking stops mattering and what gender they are starts mattering. मैं था and मैं थी are both correct, and which one you say depends on you.

examples.note: The same pronoun, two forms, decided by the speaker.
Again the pronoun does not change; the verb does all the work.
Plural, and still split by gender.

common_error.why_en: मैं is singular, so the verb is था or थी depending on the speaker, and never थे.

practice.question: कुर्सियाँ खाली ___।
practice.explanation_en: कुर्सियाँ is feminine and plural, so the verb is थीं.

game.question_en: Which pairing of subject and verb is correct?
game.explanation_en: चाय is feminine and singular, so थी. किताब would also need थी, and बच्चे needs थे.

items.pronunciation_notes: Both are single syllables at the end of the sentence, and in speech they carry very little stress.
items.gloss_en: turning a present sentence into a past one

learn.explanation_en: Turning a present sentence into a past one is mostly a matter of replacing the final word: चाय गरम है becomes चाय गरम थी. But look at what had to change. है ignored the gender of चाय entirely, while थी does not. So the swap is not one for one, and the habit to build is checking the subject's gender before you reach for a past form — a step the present tense never asked of you.

examples.note: Present, and the verb is blind to gender.
Past, and now the verb agrees as well.
A feminine subject changes both the adjective and the verb.

common_error.why_en: The adjective was made feminine but the verb was left masculine; both have to agree with चाय.

practice.prompt_en: Complete the sentence in the past tense.
practice.question: दूध ठंडा ___।
practice.explanation_en: दूध is masculine and singular, so the past form is था.

game.question_en: Which sentence is the past of चाय ठंडी है?
game.explanation_en: चाय is feminine, so the adjective is ठंडी and the verb is थी. Only one option has both.

summary.recap_en: This level completed the past forms and set the two tenses side by side. The present is decided by person and ignores gender; the past is decided by gender and number and ignores person.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the pronouns themselves, and the first short conversation.

items.pronunciation_notes: The dot nasalises the open ऐ, so the word ends in a hum: maiṁ, one syllable.

learn.explanation_en: मैं is I. It takes हूँ in the present, and था or थी in the past depending on the speaker's own gender — the pronoun itself never changes shape. It is very often left out altogether, because हूँ can belong to nothing else: यहाँ हूँ already means 'I am here'. Dropping it is ordinary rather than casual, and you will hear it done constantly.

examples.note: The full form, with the pronoun stated.
खुश does not change for gender, so this works for anyone.
अच्छा takes -ी when the speaker is female.

practice.question: ___ यहाँ हूँ।
practice.explanation_en: हूँ belongs to मैं alone, so the subject is settled by the verb.

items.pronunciation_notes: A dental त with the tongue on the teeth, and the final vowel drops: tum, one syllable.

learn.explanation_en: तुम is the everyday 'you' for friends, family, children and people of about your own age. It takes हो in the present and थे or थीं in the past, and grammatically it behaves as a plural even when you are speaking to one person — which is why the adjective in तुम अच्छे हो carries a plural ending. Hindi has three words for 'you', and choosing between them is a social decision rather than a grammatical one.

examples.note: तुम takes हो.
The everyday greeting between friends.
Plural agreement, even for a single person.

common_error.why_en: तुम takes हो. है belongs to the third person.

practice.question: ___ कहाँ हो?
practice.explanation_en: हो belongs to तुम alone, so the verb settles the subject.

game.explanation_en: तुम takes हो. हैं would be right after आप, but not after तुम.

items.pronunciation_notes: Both vowels are long and the final प releases no breath: aap.
items.setting_en: Two people meeting at a tea stall

learn.explanation_en: आप is the polite 'you', used with elders, strangers, teachers and anyone you want to show respect to. It always takes हैं in the present and थे or थीं in the past, exactly as a plural would, however many people you are addressing. When in doubt as a learner, use आप: being too polite costs you nothing, while being too familiar can land badly.

lines.speaker: A
lines.hindi: मैं भी अच्छा हूँ। चाय गरम है।
lines.read_as: maiṁ bhii achchhaa huuṁ. chaay garam hai.
lines.english: I'm well too. The tea is hot.

common_error.why_en: आप always takes हैं. हो belongs with तुम, and using it with आप sounds too familiar.

practice.question: मैं अच्छा ___।
practice.explanation_en: मैं takes हूँ, whatever else is in the sentence.

game.question_en: Listen to the first line. Which word is missing?
game.mask_reason: the form of होना required by आप
game.explanation_en: आप always takes हैं, even when only one person is being addressed.

tts_strings: मैं भी अच्छा हूँ। चाय गरम है।

summary.recap_en: This level introduced मैं, तुम and आप, and put them into a first conversation. Each takes its own form of होना — हूँ, हो and हैं — and choosing between तुम and आप is a matter of social distance rather than grammar.
summary.next_up_en: Next: तू, हम and यह, and the warning that comes with तू.
